turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come in, have a seat. What's been going on?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh it's this cough, doctor. I had the flu, proper crook, and the cough just never packed it in. My husband reckons I'm keeping the whole house awake.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long has the cough been there?

[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Six weeks, easy. Started right when the flu hit, and the flu itself was only a few days. I was off the tools for a bit, I'm a sparky, and the boss was not thrilled, but anyway.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Is it worse at any particular time?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Nights, definitely. I lie down and it starts up. Daytime I can mostly get on with things, apart from the odd fit if I'm talking too much, like now, sorry.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Are you bringing up any phlegm?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, a bit in the mornings. Whitish, not much. Not the green stuff. I thought it was just the tail of the flu, you know how it hangs around.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any blood in it?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that. I'd have been in here quicker if there was.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Fever at the moment?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No, not now. I was hot and shivery with the flu, but that's gone.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Night sweats?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I kick the doona off because I'm coughing, not because I'm sweating. Our bedroom's warm anyway, the heater's dodgy.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any weight loss?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No, I'm eating fine. My husband does a big roast most Sundays, and I don't skip brekkie.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Breathless?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): A little, yeah, on the stairs at the units. Flat ground I'm alright. I blamed being unfit, I haven't been to the gym since before the flu.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Chest pain?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No chest pain.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke?

[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): I used to. Gave it up five years ago, used to be about ten a day. My sister still smokes, and she's onto those biotin gummies for her hair, swears by them, which is mad because she won't quit the durries.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any regular medicines?

[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Ventolin puffer, two puffs if I get wheezy, not every day. And a blood pressure tablet, amlodipine, I take that every morning. My husband's the one on metformin, for his diabetes, not me. I get them mixed up in the cupboard sometimes, different bottles though.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): The nurse has written amlodipine five milligrams. Is that what you take?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Nah, that's the old dose. She must've copied last year's script. I'm on ten milligrams. Been on ten since the chemist changed it over, oh, last winter.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Every day, no missed doses?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, every morning with breakfast. I don't muck about with the blood pressure one. The puffer I only grab if I'm tight.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Penicillin. I come out in a rash. Found out years ago, I stay away from it.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any travel lately?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Haven't been out of Adelaide. We were going to drive up to Queensland in the school holidays and then the flu knocked that on the head. Maybe next year.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any contact with tuberculosis, or anyone being treated for it?

[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nobody I see. I mean, my sister was banging on about our cousin in Whyalla, she reckons he was in hospital with TB, but I haven't seen him since the Christmas before last, so I don't really count that. She dramatises everything.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. So no direct contact that you know of.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, none. If she's even right about what he had. Could've been pneumonia, she wasn't sure when I asked her back.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll have a listen to your chest. Deep breaths.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. I always cough when people do that, sorry.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Chest is clear. No wheeze and no crackles. Your throat isn't particularly red.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Feels rattly from my side though, mainly at night.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Pulse 76, oxygen 98 percent, temperature 36.7, blood pressure 132 over 78, respiratory rate 16.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Better than the chemist machine after a coffee. Those things always read high on me.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm ordering a chest X-ray. I'm not putting a name on the cause today.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): An X-ray? My uncle had a shadow on the lung, but he was a miner in Bendigo, years ago, totally different bloke.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm not saying that. Six weeks is long enough to want a film, that's all.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Should I keep using the Ventolin in the meantime?
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes. Two puffs when you're wheezy, same as now. If you cough up blood or you can't catch your breath, go to emergency, don't wait.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Yep. Oh, and the weight thing, I said I hadn't lost any, but my work pants are hanging off. Belt's in two notches. Noticed last week.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): How much weight do you think you've lost?
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): No idea of a number. Bathroom scales have been broken since Easter, so I can't check.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alright. Come back in a week, once the X-ray is back. Book it at the desk.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): Even if the cough eases a bit?
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes, in a week regardless. I want to see the film with you.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): Will do. And your nurse has me on five milligrams, that's wrong, I'm on ten, don't let that stick.
[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): I won't write either dose as fact. The chart will say it's disputed.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): Good. Thanks, doc. I'll try not to cough on the tram.

spec.situation: Cough for six weeks after flu; worse at night; patient says no weight loss, then says clothes are loose; recent travel or TB contact denied by patient but a family member recalls a cousin's illness; doctor orders chest X-ray, avoids naming a cause.
features: third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.
disputed_numbers: the nurse reads a value and the patient or relative disagrees or remembers another (a dose, a weight, a BP). Keep both and record an uncertainty.

bad.reason: Husband's diabetes is not family history for the patient.
Possible TB in cousin mentioned, but patient had no direct knowledge and relation isn't family history relevance.
Doctor said throat isn't particularly red, not clearly absent redness.
Continue salbutamol two puffs when wheezy is stated; 'do not start any new medicine' is not said.
bad.text: Continue salbutamol two puffs when wheezy and do not start any new medicine (action_type=counselling, status=recommended, responsible_person=patient)

omissions.text: Amlodipine dose is reported by the patient as 10 mg every morning; the recorded medication entry for amlodipine is missing the dose, and 5 mg was specifically stated to be an old dose from last year.
Cough is triggered by talking too much, with daytime otherwise mostly manageable apart from the odd coughing fit.

Weight loss was initially denied, but later the patient reported possible unquantified weight loss: work pants hanging off and belt in two notches, noticed last week. This creates a contradiction with the earlier recorded negative finding of no weight loss.
Examination finding that the chest was clear was stated by the doctor and is not explicitly recorded.
Follow-up was specified as in one week regardless of whether the cough eases, because the doctor wants to review the chest X-ray with the patient.
The doctor explicitly said they were not putting a name on the cause today, indicating diagnostic uncertainty beyond just ordering the X-ray.
